title: Run a probability experiment and record results with tallies

lesson.title: Try It and Tally It!

steps.say: You already know how to look at a spinner and guess what will happen. Today we learn what to do after we actually spin it — how to keep track of every single spin so we do not lose count.

visual.caption: A spinner with four equal parts: two red, one blue, one green

steps.say: Here is the trick. Every time you spin, you make one little line in a table. Four lines standing up, then the fifth line goes across them like a gate. That way you can count by fives super fast. Four lines and a slash always means five.

visual.caption: Four lines plus one across equals five — one bundle

steps.say: Maya at her school in Surrey spun this spinner twenty times at recess. Every spin, she made one mark. When she finished, she counted her bundles. Red got twelve spins, blue got five spins, and green got three spins. Let us check her work: twelve plus five plus three is twenty. That matches her twenty spins, so nothing got lost.

Now here is a mistake lots of kids make. Maya's friend Owen spun only four times and got red, red, red, blue. He shouted that the spinner is broken because green never came up! But four spins is way too few to decide anything. Green only takes up one part out of four, so missing it in four tries is totally normal. When Owen kept spinning up to twenty times, green showed up three times, just like we expected.

visual.caption: Owen's four spins — too few to judge the spinner

steps.say: So remember two things. Mark one tally for every single try, and do lots of tries before you say anything about the spinner. A few tries can trick you, but many tries tell the truth.

visual.caption: Twenty spins gives a much clearer picture

lesson.answer: One tally mark for every try, bundle them in fives, and always do lots of tries before you decide anything.

practice.question: Leo rolls a die during math club in Kamloops. He makes a tally table with three rows: 'one or two', 'three or four', and 'five or six'. When he stops, the first row has three bundles of five plus two extra marks, the second row has two bundles of five plus four extra marks, and the third row has two bundles of five plus one extra mark. Draw this table yourself. How many times did Leo land in each row, and how many times did he roll the die in total?
practice.answer: One or two: three fives is fifteen, plus two more is 17. Three or four: two fives is ten, plus four more is 14. Five or six: two fives is ten, plus one more is 11. In total, 17 + 14 + 11 = 42 rolls.
